opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the cleanest way to see it is that next-token prediction is really just a special case of distillation. In standard pretraining, you minimize cross-entropy against a one-hot target: the token that actually appeared in the data. You can think of that as distilling from a "teacher" that's a degenerate distribution, all its probability mass on one token. Logit-based distillation replaces that one-hot target with the teacher's full distribution over the vocabulary, and you minimize something like a KL divergence between the teacher's and student's next-token distributions.

Why does that matter? A one-hot label throws away a lot of information. If the next word is "car," the data doesn't tell you that "vehicle" or "automobile" were also perfectly reasonable, or that "banana" was absurd. The teacher's soft distribution carries all that "dark knowledge," so each token gives you a much richer training signal. That's a big reason distilled small models can be so much more sample efficient than training the same model from scratch on raw data.

The other piece I find really interesting is *where* the sequences come from. Classic distillation, and plain next-token prediction, is off-policy: the student trains on prefixes from a fixed dataset or from the teacher. At inference time, though, the student conditions on its own generations, so you get train-test mismatch. Small errors compound because the student never learned to recover from states it put itself in. That was the motivation behind on-policy distillation, which we worked on in the generalized knowledge distillation (GKD) work. You sample sequences from the student, then ask the teacher for its token-level distribution on those student-generated prefixes. It's very similar in spirit to imitation learning, like DAgger, where you query the expert on the states the learner actually visits.

Once you're on-policy, the choice of divergence starts to matter a lot. Forward KL, which is what next-token prediction effectively does, is mode-covering. It pushes the student to put mass everywhere the teacher does, and a small-capacity student might not be able to do that well, so you get these smeared-out, low-quality samples. Reverse KL is more mode-seeking: the student commits to the high-probability regions it can actually represent. Generalized JSD lets you interpolate between the two. In practice, which one works best depends on the task and how big the capacity gap is between teacher and student.

So the summary I'd give is: next-token prediction is distillation from the data with hard labels and off-policy sequences. Logit distillation upgrades the labels to soft ones. On-policy distillation also fixes the distribution mismatch. And at that point it starts to look a lot like RL with a very dense, per-token reward from the teacher, which I think is why there's so much interest right now in blending distillation and RL for post-training.

r001.rationale: The response says logit-based distillation replaces the one-hot target with the teacher’s full distribution over the vocabulary.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes standard cross-entropy from distillation using a KL divergence; it does not say they use the same loss.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to think about it is that next-token prediction is just a special case of distillation where the teacher is a one-hot distribution. When you do standard supervised fine-tuning or pretraining, you're minimizing cross-entropy against a delta function at the ground-truth token. Logit-based distillation replaces that delta with the full softmax of the teacher, and now you're minimizing a KL between the teacher's distribution and the student's. Same loss family, same machinery, just a richer target.

And the richness matters a lot. A one-hot target throws away everything except "this token was right." The teacher's distribution tells you that at this position, three or four continuations were all reasonable, and here's how they rank. That's the "dark knowledge" argument from the original Hinton paper, and it holds up surprisingly well for LLMs. You get a much denser learning signal per token, because every logit carries information rather than just one. In practice, that's part of why models like Gemma get so much from distillation relative to what the same compute would give you on raw next-token prediction.

Where it gets more interesting is when you ask what distribution you're actually matching. Classic logit distillation is done on a fixed dataset, so the student only sees the teacher's opinions on tokens that appear in the data. But at inference time the student is generating its own tokens, and it drifts into states the data never covered. That's the train-inference mismatch, the exposure bias story, and it's the thing that motivated on-policy distillation in our GKD work. You sample from the student, have the teacher score those samples, and minimize the divergence there. Now the student gets feedback precisely where it makes mistakes, instead of only where the data happened to go.

So I'd summarize it as a spectrum. On one end, next-token prediction on human data: hard labels, off-policy. In the middle, sequence-level distillation where you fine-tune on teacher generations, which is still hard labels but on teacher-shaped data. Then logit distillation, which gives you soft labels. And on the far end, on-policy logit distillation, which gives you soft labels on the student's own trajectories. Each step is adding information or correcting a distributional mismatch, and the loss itself barely changes. What changes is who you're asking and where.

One more nuance I'd flag is the choice of divergence. Forward KL, which is what next-token prediction implicitly uses, is mode-covering. If the student is much smaller than the teacher, it can't cover everything, and forward KL makes it spread its mass over regions it can't really represent. Reverse KL or something like a Jensen-Shannon divergence lets it be mode-seeking, which often gives you better samples from a capacity-limited student. That's something you just can't express with hard labels, because the divergence choice only becomes meaningful when the target is a full distribution.

r001.rationale: It says distillation replaces the ground-truth one-hot target with the teacher’s full softmax distribution over next-token continuations.

r002.rationale: It connects both objectives as the same loss family: cross-entropy against a hard target for next-token prediction and KL against the teacher distribution for distillation.

astra-6.text:
I think of logit-based distillation as next-token prediction with a richer target. In standard training, you see a context and one token that actually followed it, and you train the model to put probability on that token. With distillation, you instead train against the teacher’s distribution over possible next tokens.

The objective is still predicting what comes next. What changes is the supervision: the teacher can tell you that several continuations are plausible, and how plausible they are relative to one another. You usually express that as minimizing cross-entropy or KL divergence between the teacher’s and student’s distributions.

There’s also a useful distinction between training on text generated by a teacher and training on its logits. If you only use generated text, you’re doing ordinary next-token prediction on samples from the teacher. If you have the logits, you get information about alternatives that weren’t sampled. So they’re closely related, but the amount of information you get at each token is different.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the single observed next token in standard training with distillation against the teacher’s distribution over possible next tokens.

r002.rationale: It says the objective is still next-token prediction and mentions cross-entropy or KL for distillation, but does not state that distillation uses the same loss function as standard next-token prediction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of logit-based distillation as next-token prediction with a different target distribution. In standard next-token training, you observe one token from the data and maximize its probability. With distillation, the teacher gives you a distribution over possible next tokens, and you train the student to match that distribution, typically by minimizing a KL divergence.

That gives you a richer learning signal: instead of just saying, “This token occurred,” the teacher tells you which alternatives it considers plausible and their relative probabilities. But the student is still learning an autoregressive next-token predictor; the underlying prediction problem hasn’t changed.

There’s also a useful connection to training on generated text. If you sample a token from the teacher and train on it with ordinary next-token cross-entropy, then, in expectation, you’re optimizing the same cross-entropy against the teacher’s distribution. Using the full logits gives you that signal directly rather than estimating it from samples. In practice, the contexts you train on, the sampling procedure, and whether those contexts come from the student or the teacher can make a big difference.

r001.rationale: It contrasts standard training’s single observed token with distillation’s teacher-provided distribution over possible next tokens.

r002.rationale: It says distillation typically minimizes KL divergence and only describes cross-entropy equivalence for training on sampled teacher tokens; it does not clearly state that logit-based distillation uses the same loss function as standard next-token prediction.
